All Headings.title: <h1> to <h6> — The Content Hierarchy Blueprint
All Headings.history:
The foundational roadmap that structures your website's topics for readers and search bots.

Heading tags range from <h1> (most important) to <h6> (least important). They are not meant to make text look big or bold—that is CSS's job. Instead, they act as the index of your page, mapping out sections so web crawlers and screen readers can instantly digest the logical architecture of your content layout.
All Headings.tip: The Strict SEO Golden Rule: Never use more than one <h1> tag on a single webpage! Think of your <h1> as the book title, and <h2> through <h6> as chapters and sub-sections. Breaking this order confuses Google's indexing spiders and hurts your ranking.

em.title: <em> — The Voice Stress & Emphasis Tag
em.history:
Tells browsers, screen readers, and search engines where to put the acoustic weight in a sentence.

The <em> element is a semantic formatting tag used to emphasize words. While it physically renders text in italics by default, its true purpose is programmatic. It visually changes the tone of the sentence, changing how a text-to-speech screen reader verbally pronounces the word to a visually impaired user.
em.tip: The Semantics Rule (em vs. i): Never use <em> just to make text look pretty and slanted—use CSS font-style: italic; or the <i> tag for that! Use <em> only when changing the word's stress actually changes the meaning of the spoken sentence.

hr.title: <hr> — The Thematic Break & Divider Tag
hr.history:
Tells browsers, screen readers, and layout engines how to inject a clean structural or thematic break between blocks of content.

The <hr> element is a semantic structural tag used to separate sections of a document. While it physically renders as a simple gray horizontal line by default, its true purpose is programmatic. It creates a formal divider in the document outline, signaling a shift in topic or a transition in the narrative flow for both search engines and assistive screen readers.
hr.tip: The Semantics Rule (hr vs. border): Never use <hr> just to create random decorative lines or boxes—use CSS border-top or border-bottom properties for that! Use <hr> only when a genuine transition or thematic shift occurs between two distinct blocks of content.

h2.title: <h2> — The Section Subheading Tag
h2.history:
Tells browsers, search engines, and screen readers how to map the primary structural sections of your webpage content.

The <h2> element is a semantic typography tag used to define level-2 headings. While it physically renders text in a larger, bolder font by default, its true purpose is programmatic. It establishes a clear content hierarchy, allowing search engine crawlers to index your page topics accurately and enabling screen reader users to jump directly to major sections of your layout.
h2.tip: The Hierarchy Rule (h1 vs. h2): Never use <h2> tags out of numerical order or just to make text bold—use CSS font-weight: bold; for visual styling! Use <h2> only to start a new subsection directly beneath a top-level <h1> heading, ensuring a logical document outline.
